items.title: 12.2.3 Synthesis of ammonia from ammonium salts

source_refs.note: Topic 12.2.3 with Figure 12.3, printed page 275. The printed product 'NaCl' is read as calcium chloride and noted.

blocks.text: In the laboratory ammonia gas is made by heating an ammonium salt such as ammonium chloride with a base such as calcium hydroxide (Figure 12.3): 2NH4Cl(s) + Ca(OH)2 gives CaCl2 + 2H2O(l) + 2NH3(g) (the print writes the salt as NaCl). In this acid-base reaction NH4+ acts as an acid by donating H+ and OH- as a base by accepting it; the reaction displaces ammonia gas from the ammonium salt and leaves a salt and water. It is commonly used to identify ammonium in salt analysis: a gas with a pungent smell that turns moist red litmus paper blue indicates ammonium in the compound.

blocks.prompt: A farmer should not apply an ammonium fertiliser and lime to a field at the same time. Why, and what reaction occurs (Quick Check 12.1c)?
blocks.explanation: Lime is a base (CaO or Ca(OH)2); with ammonium sulfate it releases the nitrogen as ammonia gas, which escapes: (NH4)2SO4 + Ca(OH)2 gives CaSO4 + 2H2O + 2NH3. The fertiliser's nitrogen is lost to the air instead of feeding the crop.

items: Heat an ammonium salt with a base: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 gives CaCl2 + 2H2O + 2NH3; NH4+ is the acid, OH- the base; pungent gas turning damp red litmus blue identifies ammonium.
